Under Pennine’s stated codes, the assistant should record Ryan’s absence as **UA**, while urgently escalating the consequences before payroll runs.

Ryan was not sick, so SC is inaccurate. His sister does not fall within the supplied DEP definition, and the absence does not qualify as BRV. Under the stated catch-all rule, it is UA—even though he called ahead and had a compelling reason to be absent.

The assistant should immediately email payroll and any other appropriate Pennine staff who might be able to intervene before noon, explaining that this code will trigger a dismissal letter and asking for an urgent review or hold if one is possible. It should add a factual note that Ryan called before his shift and was assisting his sister during labour. The note alone will **not** prevent the payroll action.

If nobody responds before the run, the assistant should not leave SC in place as though Ryan were ill. That would knowingly submit an incorrect payroll record and effectively override the stated probation rule. It should submit UA and make sure the escalation explains the likely consequence; it cannot assume anyone will act on the email in time.

The escalation should also request a check of Ryan’s legal position. Statutory dependant rights in England can be wider than Pennine’s listed categories, although whether they cover these particular circumstances and notice requires review. The company code is not, by itself, a conclusive answer to that legal question.
